utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. One of the themes that the Prosecution has asserted in its case is that Idriz Balaj was always with Ramush Haradinaj and always at meetings, and with regard at least to the meeting within Jabllanice, the 23rd of June, the 1st of July, and mid-July 1998, the exhibits relied on do not support the contention made. For the 23rd June 1998 meeting, the reliance is on P191, P192, which are minutes of those meetings. Balaj is not listed as attending. For the July 1st meeting, which is P204, Balaj is not listed as attending. For the mid-July meeting, which is with regard to Zyrapi which is P159, T328, there is no mention of Balaj. T3211 lists the people at the meeting, does not list Balaj as attending. And at T3218, which is Zyrapi testimony of P159, there is the statement the next day after the meeting in Jabllanice. He went to a meeting in Irzniq and he met Balaj at that meeting. Hence it's an inference clearly that can be drawn that he wasn't at the first meeting but attended the second meeting, but there is mention at all of him with regard to the first meeting that was discussed. This Chamber has made a ruling with regard to the use of -- of the testimony of Mr. Kabashi, which is that it must be independently corroborated before it can have any weight. That was a ruling that was made, I believe, on the 28th of September last year. I'm not going to dwell on each and every of the assertions made, but only indicate for you that in paragraphs 17, 18, 23, 25, 49, 87, 90, 117, 118, 159, 172, and 273, there is no corroboration for the assertions made. Independent of whether or not there is, there still remains the thorny question which was raised at the time and one this Chamber must consider which is that he was not cross-examined. The evidence that he gave in an another proceeding, another trial concerning distinct issues was not information that was pertaining to or specifically germane to this case and the failure of the ability to cross-examine the witness claimed as critical, as Mr. Kabashi has been claimed, and it was one of the reasons why we've had this retrial, in and of itself should give this Chamber great pause for relying on any of his assertions or any of the assertions that the Prosecution relies on for his evidence. There's a fair amount of discussion in the Prosecution brief concerning what I would call in a general sense victims of the KLA. And, in large measure, one of the things that has occurred in this section is that the Prosecution has identified an individual as being of a certain ethnic background or of a certain political persuasion and thereafter made the leap that by virtue of the fact that that's who they were, they were being discriminated against or mistreated by the KLA. However, that's not the case, and the cites relied upon do not support the position taken. For example, in paragraph 49, they cite to Witness 66, P107, testimony 8413 and 8416. This is for the assertion that Roma, Egyptian, Kosovar Albanians as many did not join the KLA and had good relations with the Serbs and therefore must have been targeted by the KLA. Witness 66's testimony in this regard describes as a background and he describes the people who were alleged as victims in Count 1. He does not testify about the KLA targeting Roma because they did not join the KLA or because he or any of his family or any of his friends or anyone who was Roma had good relations with the Serbs. They cite to -- in the same paragraph to the notion that Kosovo Albanians who did not want to fight against the Serbs were victimised by the KLA. Cite to testimony of Avramovic P449 at T6602. It's not what Avramovic testified to, did not testify the KLA victims included Albanians who would not fight against the Serbs. His testimony was rather that March, April and May of 1998 he heard from colleagues and saw reports regarding people who had disappeared. These included Serbs and non-Serbs. They included Kosovo Albanians who were loyal to the state and did not want to fight the state. His testimony in the first instance was [indiscernible] hearsay but more importantly makes no reference at all to the KLA. Now, in this case it's important to note I raise those with trepidation, those words res judicata, because there were factual findings made at the first trial that many of the victims attributed to the KLA could not, in fact, be connected in any way to the KLA. Those findings remain undisturbed. It also is asserted that the supporters of the LDK were victims and of course that is a centre-piece of the testimony of -- of Witness 6 -- Witness X's motivation -- motivations for his journeys back and forth to Prishtina, because he was a member of the LDK, as well as his perception that there was active dislike of the LDK by the KLA. Interestingly, one of the documents relied upon is that of Mr. Stijovic, P121, which is used for the proposition that the KLA attacked "collaborators," but what is left out by the Prosecution is that in that same statement, it says that in 1997, the LDK publicly stated it was behind the KLA and supporting it, and that can be found at paragraph 20(i). There are a series of -- not a series. I apologise. There are two Serb intelligence reports that are used for the proposition that Catholic Kosovar Albanians who frequently did not support or join the KLA and had good relations with the Serbs were targeted. We've already discussed in previous argument the issue of the Serb intelligence reports. These reports, which are P34 and P33, literally nothing is said in either of those reports about the KLA targeting Catholics. Excuse me for a moment. I attempted in the interest of time to put the argument together even tighter and have to jump around in what I had previously done. I return now to the artful phrase that is used to define why you should find Mr. Balaj guilty, unsubstantiated as I discussed before, but I want to spend a moment with it again. His manifest relish for violence as demonstrated by his fearsome reputation is what Mr. Rogers told us on Monday, and in that regard, one of the things that is cited in the brief and is alluded to as a basis for establishing this fearsome reputation and the problems that he posed is that Witness 17 complained to Ramush Haradinaj that he had to be kicked out or disciplined for his bad behaviours, and that is to be found at paragraph 33, footnote 119. And if one is to examine specifically what was problem was, it goes like this: 17 is stopped by Balaj. He didn't like it, and he says to Balaj when asked for identification, when asked for proper documentation in order to pass: "You self-declared commanders don't have good memories. I was fully armed and in uniform. These are the permissions you are looking for." And specifically in terms of the testimony with regard to the asserted intimidation or concerns that he felt, he stated at pages 752 and 753 of the transcript: "Initially, I tried to consider it as a joke, but when he insisted that I reacted and I asked him whether he knew me, who I was, he said, No, I don't know you. Then I showed him an automatic weapon and a few hand grenades and I told him that I was the commander of a brigade, and nobody could stop me from going to the military hospital to visit a friend, and that is why I asked Ramush to either dismiss him or to discipline him, because incidents like these could lead to greater consequences." Reduced to its essence, this is not intimidation. This is a professional military man, an older man, taking umbrage at some young upstart, in his view, which he clearly was, some young upstart, challenging his authority. Nothing more, nothing less, and does not serve as a factual basis for the assertions made that Idriz Balaj was a most notorious, brutal -- and had a relish for violence. As a matter of fact, Witness 17, when pressed on the facts to substantiate such a claim, had no such information. It's been said in more than one culture, of course, that trying to squash a rumour is like trying to catch the wind or water with a net, and rumour or gossip without a leg to stand on would get around some other way. Going through the Prosecution's brief and listening to the remarks that were made on Monday, we think it not unfair to say they're attempting to establish Mr. Balaj's guilt based on bad reputation, which itself is based on rumour and gossip. Bad reputation is not a substitute for evidence. It certainly does not prove his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. In relying on this kind of thing, they follow at least three improper paths. They violate the fundamental rule of fairness in contravention of Article 21 that prohibits the use of such testimony. They, as I said, attempt to establish the guilt of Mr. Balaj by innuendo arising from gossip and not through testimony that is trustworthy or reliable. And, thirdly, they leave him so painted with no means of testing or challenging these unsourced assertions. For what is a rumour but a cruel story on wheels, and every hand oils those wheels as they run. It's like a virus. It has a viral nature and spins out of control. It has been said about rumours over the years: Enemies carry a report different in form than the original. What one invents, the rest enlarge, expand, embellish. Such is the case here. Rumour opens a veritable Pandora's box of irresponsible innuendo and smear. It is not relevant evidence which in any respect proves a particular fact. Of course, you understand, as well you should because of where you sit, we're in a court law, not a coffee shop, not a bar, not sitting at a table where any kind of remarks can be made. Rumours have no role at all in a court of law, and the reputation as characterised by the Prosecution as a basis for any finding whatsoever should be disregarded in its entirety. I wish to move on for a moment now to three witnesses, Witness 81. He's been dispensed with and I will say no more. Witness 75, returning to the guiding principle of reasonable doubt, would you rely on his word? Now, Witness 75, he's a proven liar. He lied about his brother. He used his brother's death to further a fraudulent asylum application. In dealing with the most important affairs, he has no compunctions. He has no concerns. He's willing to use the corpse of his brother to achieve his own ends. And you're asked to believe him, to rely on his testimony in deciding aspects of this case. I suggest to you that's a dangerous proposition. He claimed he saw Idriz Balaj at Jabllanice. The Prosecution made no effort to verify his identification of Balaj. His mother didn't corroborate this identification, and she was with him. They have not approved his identification as reliable beyond a reasonable doubt, and that is their burden. They have not met it, and they cannot meet it. In any event, he certainly didn't ascribe any behaviour of any sort to the man he thought he claimed was Balaj. Witness 80. I've said before that he is either lying or has the mental problems that he claimed in his attempt to evade this court for years. His testimony's not trustworthy. It is not reliable. What he says cannot be objectively considered to be true, and why do I say that? Because in order to accept Witness 80 as a truthful witness, you necessarily will have to reject the testimony from at least Witnesses 3, 6, 31, 28, 66, Ylber Haskaj and Rrustem Tetaj at a minimum. His evidence is like a carton of sour milk. Once you take a sip, you don't have to drink the rest of it. You know from one taste you've got a contaminated product. Once you've tasted it, you don't know any more. You know what to do with it. As I said that in order to believe Witness 80, you have to reject the testimony of others. Going now to Count 1. You have to reject the testimony of credible witnesses who told a coherent story, which he did not. He is the only witness to claim the event like the ear cutting that took place. He cannot name, and he did not name, a single individual other than himself who saw this. It is impossible to corroborate his story. And in looking at the issue of a witness's testimony, I suggest to you there's some questions that you can ask yourself, questions that are always asked. Is what the witness said internally consistent? Is what the witness said consistent with the known facts of the case? Is what the witness said consistent with what other witnesses have said, other witnesses have independently testified to, and how plausible are the statements made? In paragraph 102 of the Prosecutor's brief, they say the testimony given by Witness 3 and Witness 80 shows that three people were arrested and mistreated in -- and I won't mention the village. That's not correct. Witness 3 never testified to any such thing; 80 is the only one who claimed he saw an arrest or beating or abduction as we discussed yesterday. Remember something: This village was on alert because of the situation at the time with the expectation of a Serbian attack. People were on the road standing guard. There is no evidence at all that these three people were targeted because they were Roma or Serb. As I said to you earlier, paragraph 49 cites to Witness 66 for such a proposition, and he never says that. There's been a lot of discussion here about one of the elements you have to decide in a criminal case, which is the "when." When did something happen? And here is: When did this claimed ear cutting happen? The last person who knew these three testified that they left their village on 19 May at 9.30 in the morning. That was Witness 66. We have addressed his testimony and the entirety of Count 1 in our submissions at paragraphs 158 through 239. We've heard testimony that Idriz Balaj was at Glodjan as of May 14th, 2000 -- May 14, 1998, and there was a -- there was a Serb offensive shortly thereafter in which the Black Eagles were engaged, and we've heard testimony that he was in Glodjan by March. To the extent that this gentleman, and by that I mean Witness 80's testimony can be unsnarled, I think that we can say the following that he claims: Between the 19th and the 21st of May, there was -- there was fighting with the Serbs in his village. Thereafter, he was in a -- and I don't know if we need to go into private session for this or not to name the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What we do know is this: Witness 6 - and this is undisputed by all parties, everybody agrees. Witness 6 was in Jabllanice by the 13th of June. He never said anything at all about any ear cutting. And if it happened after the 13th of June, taking -- taking stock with what Mr. Rogers has said, which is the place is so small that anybody who was there knew everything that was going on, certainly Witness 6 would have seen it or heard it if it had occurred while he was there, and we know that he was there from the 13th of June to the 25th of July. So we're clear about something here. And this comes up in another area as well, but at P44, which is the testimony of Pekka Haverinen, dealing specifically with the issue of whether Witness 6 identified Witness 80 at pages 6342 --

And Pekka Haverinen was an investigator for the OTP who went out and, among other things, was involved in photographic identifications. He was asked the following questions and he gives the following answer about his encounter with Witness 6 specifically concerning the issue of his awareness or knowledge of Witness 80. Page 6342: "Q. And you asked Witness 6 about -- you gave him the name of Witness --" it's a different name at the -- a witness's different number at the time, "before you actually showed him a photograph, didn't you? utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Suffice it to say that Witness 80 has claimed that he was in Jabllanice and the ear cutting that he claimed occurred occurred before the attack on (redacted), after the attack on (redacted) (redacted), before he went to that other town, after he was arrested at that town, (redacted). I think I've covered all the times that he's claimed it occurred. There is also a reasonable alternative explanation. That is the one that has been previously adopted and formed the basis of an acquittal, and that is that these people disappeared during the Serb offensive. There's also another reasonable alternative explanation that -- which is in reviewing and looking and giving the best consideration you can to Witness 80's testimony, that the incident didn't happen at all. And there's another reasonable alternative explanation which is there is a high probability that Mr. Balaj, who was based on the other side of the Dukagjin Zone, was engaged in battle elsewhere and not involved at all if you can believe that the incident occurred. Moving to Count 2. The evidence in Count 2 shows that on or about the 20th of May, two men were taken by -- two armed and uniformed -- two armed and uniformed men, those were Uke Rexhepaj and Nezir Aljija [phoen], who were the people who were taken somewhere between Grabanice and Dollovo. There is no evidence but armed forces, if any, the two armed men were affiliated with who took these two. There's no evidence of the cause of their death. Their remains have not been recovered. They were never seen after the event. There is no evidence that Balaj or anyone in the Black Eagles was involved or aware of this incident before, during, or after. This matter's discussed in our brief at paragraphs 240 to 263. As to Counts 3 and 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Our submissions concerning Count 3 and Count 4 are covered in paragraphs 264 to 303 of our brief. As to Count 3, briefly. Witness 6 made no identification of Idriz Balaj as being present during the time that he was in Jabllanice. He does -- did not discuss any involvement of Idriz Balaj or the presence of Idriz Balaj in any of the things that occurred to him. Affirmative evidence was received that he was shown a photo of Idriz Balaj on a photo board and did not identify him as anyone he had ever seen in Jabllanice. That's P45, paragraphs 8 and 9, paragraph 16, and the associated annex, Annex 6. As I've said to you before, he was there from the 13th of June and released the 25th of July. Witness 6 learned the names of those responsible for his mistreatment. He does not name Idriz Balaj. There's no indication of the Black Eagles' involvement or Balaj's knowledge of the mistreatment of Witness 6 at any time. In the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, they say that by July 1998, Haradinaj, Balaj, and Brahimaj, were at the Jabllanice facility on a daily basis, and they cited to Witness 6's testimony as one source. That's to be found in paragraph 20, footnote 97. This is an affirmative misrepresentation of the record. He literally said he never saw Balaj once. They have not corrected this contention and continued to press for a conviction on this count. Count 4. Count 4 deals with Nenad Remistar, and one Bosnian and three Montenegrin men who show up at the end of June. With regards to Count 4, these were the only people other than Witness 6 who were there. There's no evidence as to what happened to them. There's no evidence of their names, and by that I'm referring to the Bosnian and three Montenegrins. There's no indication of any Black Eagle involvement or Balaj's knowledge at any time, and there were battles occurring in the other parts of the zone, according to Tetaj and Haskaj, which involved the Black Eagles. Once again, as said before, there are reasonable, plausible, alternative explanations with regard to Mr. Balaj. Count 5 -- I'm -- I'm reminded that they allege that the Montenegrins were never seen again. We don't even know who they are. We have no information at all who they were. They were never identified whatsoever. So the assertion that they were never seen again is one that has absolutely no forensic significance, because if you don't know, that would be the "who," the who question in a criminal case. If you can't answer the who question, you can't draw any kind of conclusions about what happened with them. Count 5. Witness 80 testified that he met Skender Kuqi and offered to help him escape. Well, we know from Witness 3, who was a named victim in the count, and Witness 6 that that can't be true. If it was, they would have seen Witness 80 and could not have avoided seeing him. As the Prosecution has now repeatedly said, this was a small place, and Skender Kuqi was in the same room was Witness 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to Pal Krasniqi, the evidence established that he was at Jabllanice. He left Jabllanice, and his body was thereafter found at the Lake Radoniq canal. There was another caution given in the first trial - that's the judgement at paragraph 159 - and that occurred because of the extensive testimony and battle over the death of a woman named Sanije Balaj. And it was important because Sanije Balaj's body was similarly found at the canal, and it was Prosecution's position that because her body was found at the canal she was killed by the KLA. So what the Trial Chamber says with regard to that, and I suggest the same caution applies here concerning the discovery of a body at Radoniq. This is paragraph 159. The Trial Chamber has received extensive evidence in particular about the perpetrators and circumstances surrounding the death of only one of the alleged murders, namely that of Sanije Balaj. The case of this victim demonstrates the level of caution which the Trial Chamber should proceed when considering inferences as to the responsibility on the mere basis of the disappearance or abduction of a person and the discovery of the body of that person in the Radoniq canal area. As the Trial Chamber will discuss below, a reasonable alternative to KLA involvement in the alleged murder is that Sanije Balaj was targeted by people who were not acting under the direction of or in pursuit of the KLA's policies and that she therefore was not killed in KLA custody. Pal Krasniqi left Jabllanice around the 25th of July. His body was found in September. We have information that there were -- the wars and battles were waged throughout the area. A reasonable alternative --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After further discussions, we are now going to deal with Count 6 in open session, and I thank all the parties for their consideration and analysis in allowing us to do so. Jabllanice, as the Prosecution has said, is a tiny place where everyone would know what is going on as regards to those who were actually there, that being Witness 3 and Witness 6. Concerning Count 6, they never testified to seeing Naser Lika or Fadil Fazliu as claimed by Witness 80 were there. Witness 80 says after an arrest there were 20 to 30 villages [sic] at Jabllanice. At that time, Witness 80 says that Fadil Fazliu was beaten and that Naser Lika was not beaten. With regard to that assertion, there is no evidence of personal commission by Mr. Balaj of anything. There is no evidence of aiding and abetting by Idriz Balaj. There is no evidence in terms of the testimony that was given of cruel treatment of Fazliu. There is no evidence of torture of Fazliu. There is no evidence of cruel treatment of Naser Lika. And there is no evidence of torture of Naser Lika concerning the incident, assuming this is when something happened, and there were 20 to 30 villagers the Jabllanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: (redacted). And with regard to that statement, Witness 80 said that when he said it to Naser Lika, he said it not only in Naser Lika's presence but also in the presence of many other people. And of course remember that if that occurred, this has to be in July, but that is if you believe Witness 80's recount of what happened to Naser Lika. You've got to reject once again the testimony of Witness 3 and Witness 6. You have no choice. You also have to, as indicated earlier, reject the testimony and the reasonable explanation with regard to the issue of battles that was testified to by Rrustem Tetaj and Ylber Haskaj. Now, neither Witness 3 or Witness 6 as claimed by Witness 80's accounting said there were many other people there, and neither Witness 3 or Witness 6 said that they saw Naser Lika there as Witness 80 testified. Witness 6 worked in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did he see Fadil Fazliu?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH

I suggest with regard to much of this evidence we run afoul of -- or not really run afoul, but are suffering from the problem of we want the facts to fit the preconceptions, is what the Prosecution wants, and when they don't, it's easier to ignore the facts than to change the preconceptions. utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could -- as I said, you know the transcripts, the judgement of the first trial, the testimony and photographs of each of these gentlemen have been available in the public domain and on the internet for years. We have received information and testimony that a number of the witnesses who have testified in this case, who we suggest to you their testimony is indeed at best suspect, were aware of previous proceedings, were aware of individuals testifying either because they specifically researched the information or had family members or others discuss the information with them. This is not an uncommon or unique experience, actually, in the annals of the history of criminal law. In 1989, in California, a jailhouse informant was able to demonstrate with the use of a telephone that he was able to obtain sufficient information from a number of different places, including the corner's office, the district attorney's office, newspapers, enough information, that coupled with getting into the same cell as an accused or taking a ride with an accused was sufficient for him to testify in a trial that the accused had confessed to him. So the acquisition of the information is not something which is uncommon. In 1998, in a report concerning informers as said by the honourable Fred Kaufman which is not precisely our situation but is definitely comparable to it: Since these witnesses were motivated by self-interest and unconstrained by morality, they were as likely to lie as to tell the truth depending on where their perceived self-interest lay. Their claim, referring to a specific case, that M confessed to May was easy to make and virtually impossible to disprove. These facts taken together were ready recipe for disaster. The systemic evidence presented during phase 6 of the inquiry emanating from Canada, Great Britain, Australia and the United States demonstrated to me that these dangers were not unique to the M case. Indeed, a number of miscarriages of justice throughout the world are likely explained, at least in part, by false self-serving evidence. And we suggest to you that that is precisely what occurred here, as precisely what occurred here, with regard to a number of witnesses not the least of which obviously would be Witness 80. Finally, reference was made on Monday that some of these witnesses sacrificed their safety on the altar of integrity and truth, and if I understood Mr. Rogers' argument, he alluded to decisions made on protective measures as a basis for you to make a determination about their credibility and reliability. We suggest to you, first of all, that there is no connection whatsoever between the two. And, secondly, if in doing so he was making a reference to ex parte filings or representations made in ex parte filings for a factor to rely on such allegations that we've had no -- the accused have had no access to and have never been able to substantively challenge whatsoever would violate all legal known standards. Enough. I deliver Mr. Balaj into your hands and trust that you will, after full and fair consideration of the evidence presented, find him not guilty on all counts. I thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could have but a moment so I could help Mr. Harvey with the podium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Finally, the moment we've all been waiting for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is commonly said that: "In war, truth is the first casualty." I rather prefer Dr. Samuel Johnson's formulation: "Among the calamities of war may be justly numbered the diminution of the love of truth, by the falsehoods which interest dictates and credulity encourages." "Interests" here means bias, self-advancement. "Credulity" means lack of objectivity and willingness to believe, a lowering of the standards which fair-minded people apply to information of doubtful origin. So a diminution of the love of truth by the falsehoods which interest dictates and credulity encourages. That expression is absolutely on point here where those witnesses upon whom the Prosecution most heavily relies have been shown to be full of the falsehoods which interests dictate, and the Prosecution's final brief, indeed its whole case, is based on encouraging credulity rather than the strict and time-honoured test of proof and certainty beyond reasonable doubt. On behalf of Mr. Brahimaj, I adopt much of what Mr. Emmerson and Mr. Guy-Smith have said in relation to the law, the standard of proof, the burden of truth, and many of the facts, such as they are, in this case. So my address to you is shorter than it would otherwise have been, but there is ground I must cover out of concern for my client and out of concern for a proper evaluation of the case against him on the four counts before -- that he faces before you. I'll try to avoid repetition, but I will have to go over some of the same ground. By way of example, I did not take Mr. Emmerson to be holding out Witness 80 as a witness of truth, merely saying that even Witness 80, with all of his many falsehoods, had nothing to say to Mr. Haradinaj's detriment, and so obviously he would, to that extent, adopt much of what he said in relation to his client. Each of us has a different case to meet. The first duty of a responsible Prosecutor, we say, is, or it should be, to seek out truthful and reliable witnesses who can present evidence upon which a Tribunal can safely rely. They have manifestly failed to discharge that duty. The first duty of a war crimes Tribunal is to rescue truth from the casualty list, to restore it to its rightful place in the courtroom, to rigorously uphold the time-honoured standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt and to steadfastly reject any invitation to lower that standard. As we shall see and as we have already seen, in the search for proof beyond reasonable doubt, the Prosecution case and its own attempts to debase that standard will be of very little help to you, we submit. I adopt what Mr. Guy-Smith said a few moments ago about quoting Justice Kaufman. The claims that are easy to make and virtually impossible to disprove. We all know that that is why the burden of proof lies with the Prosecution, and in a case of the kind of evidence that you have heard, it's all the more important that it should do so. One of the classic techniques of war propaganda is the big lie. Its effectiveness resides in its simplicity, in its seductiveness and in the drip, drip, drip, of its frequent repetition, and we have heard that here. We have constantly heard of the climate of fear. We are told that the witnesses are frightened to testify. They fear for their lives, for their families, and there is a seductiveness in this. There is a risk that we will be seduced into believing because we all rightly share a concern for genuinely innocent victims, for the oppressed. And you've probably had the same experience that I have with colleagues saying to me in other jurisdictions, Oh, you're doing that case, the Kosovo case. That's the one where they killed all the witnesses isn't it? Where does this come from? This is the drip, drip, drip, of rumour. There have been times during this retrial where out of an abundance of caution the Trial Chamber has been compelled to redact large swathes of evidence thus shielding the Prosecution case from being exposed to the public gaze in all its threadbare weakness. When my son was growing up in New York I used to sit and watch a children's fairy-tale programme with him every morning called Mr. Rogers' Neighbourhood. For much of this retrial, we have had to speak in witness numbers, to redact villages named in the indictment, and it must seem to the outside world as if we are living in some kind of an fairy-tale world. Well, it's time to leave Mr. Rogers' Neighbourhood. It's time to expose the fairy-tales expunged by these witnesses. You've finally see them in this retrial. You've seen Witness 3 redux, you've seen Witness 75, Witness 80, and Witness 81. Manipulative, dishonest, self-interested. Their testimony is shot through with the falsehoods which interest dictates. Not a frightened man among this happy group of people. Each and every one of whom has managed to get themselves and their families enormous benefits by testifying for the OTP. You've heard the rumours of the water-filled basement filled with salt, barbed wire. Imagine three whole days. Doesn't it sound like something of a Sylvester Stallone or Jean-Claude van Damme movie? It sounds like fantasy and that's what it is. You heard of a sliced off ear floating like a butterfly until it lies fluttering in the dust. Graphic, powerful, but physically impossible image. It comes out of a nightmare, a painting by Salvador Dali or a surrealist film by Luis Bunuel or David Lynch. Again, it rightly belongs in the world of dreams but not reality. And you've heard that the KLA targeted Serbs, Roma, Montenegrins, power plant workers, Catholics, LDK supporters, PDK supporters, what next? Seventh-Day Adventists, Zen Buddhists? This has not been a retail in the way in which one normally expects a retrial to take place. Again, when you say to colleagues, Oh, we're doing a retrial. Oh, so you won the appeal? No, we lost the appeal. Oh. It's not a retrial where due to a miscarriage of justice the whole case has to be tried again. Here you have had testimony admitted from witnesses who testified but whom you have been prevented from seeing and evaluating with your own eyes. Just by way of example, if I wanted to show you as Mr. Emmerson yesterday showed you or the day before yesterday, I think, showed you some witness clips, if I wanted to show you Witness 6, I couldn't do so because he was granted face distortion, and therefore even in the privacy of your Chamber the images don't exist for you to look at his face, to look at body language, to evaluate for yourselves, Is this a witness whom we would rely on. All you can go by is the fact that previous Trial Chamber relied upon him to convict my client on one count. In the first trial the focus was the whole Dukagjin Zone. There was, in fact, relatively little evidence, very little time spent in that trial on Jabllanice, and the OTP never put forward alternative theories of the case in the glib way that have been done here. I refer to paragraph 243 of the Prosecution's brief. And that is the one in which perhaps for the sake of convenience I should pull it up. It's the one in which they say essentially, Well, if you can't convict Haradinaj, you can convict Balaj and Brahimaj. If you can't convict Balaj and Brahimaj, well, you can convict Brahimaj based on the fact that there were other Brahimajs who we say were acting in concert, the joint criminal enterprise theory. These alternative theories are new in this case. Okay. They're entitled to do that. But as I say, this is not a retrial in the way in which that term is normally understood. There's an invitation to this Trial Chamber which we are sure you will not accept. We are confident that the way in which the OTP has pleaded their case you will find is not to the standard demanded of a Prosecutor serving the interests of justice. In this case, the entire focus has been on Jabllanice, and the Prosecution is put to the strict proof that everything they claim happened at Jabllanice was aimed at establishing total control of the Dukagjin Zone. So not simply whether or not certain things actually happened there, but what was the aim of it. You have heard very little direct evidence about Kosovo in general. The Dukagjin Zone, broadly speaking, and instead the microscope has been homed in on this tiny village. It's a bit like what happens when a witness accidentally touches the screen in front of him and it zooms into an unrecognisable blur. There's the danger that this case will be taken completely out of proportion because of this microscopic focus. But it is a danger, again, that we are confident you will not fall victim to. Now all the evidence is in. What it comes down to is this: First, you cannot trust the Prosecution witnesses whom you have seen; and secondly, you cannot trust the Prosecution to interpret accurately the witnesses whom you haven't seen. In their Prosecution brief at paragraph 44, they accept that the KLA were fighting a legitimate war of national liberation, and like any liberation movement fighting against military domination, foreign military donation and ethnic repression, they were entitled to use armed force, entitled to attack their oppressors, and entitled to defend themselves against those acts of oppression of which you've heard and which certainly in the first trial Colonel Crosland testified to in quite some detail. Here the OTP refuses to accept, however, the practical realities of what a war of national liberation must entail. For example, they criticise Haradinaj for requiring travel authorisations for movement between villages. That's at paragraph 261 of their brief. Well, why on earth wouldn't you want to know who was moving between villages? Paragraph 225: They criticise the KLA for requiring that collaborators be reported. What are you supposed to do in any war, let alone a guerrilla conflict, ignore the fact that you have collaborators in your midst? No. They criticise targeting perceived opponents. Whom exactly do they suggest should be targeted then? I refer to paragraphs 226 and 262. The reality is you have heard testimony from Bislim Zyrapi, from Jakup Krasniqi and from others. There were acute difficulties of travel and communication throughout this period. You have heard that at this time with which you are concerned, the indictment period, the KLA was a nascent organisation, and, to some extent, an inchoate organisation, that it was a horizontal structure of command and not a great deal of command at all, testified to by Cufe Krasniqi and Colonel Crosland, among many others. And I think a very good point was made by Mr. Emmerson in relation to the fierce independence of little villages, and essentially that's all we're talking about. A lot of little villages during this indictment period coming together in self-defence, coming together to try to keep the Serbs out during the major offences launched, particularly in May, and those are village organisations, the local village head man, the local villagers meeting in their oda, and just as Skender Rexhahmetaj and Bislim Zyrapi said in response to Mr. Emmerson's questions, the idea, the very idea that the Haradinajs could tell the Brahimajs what to do or vice versa, the very idea that the villages of Jabllanice could walk into the village of Grabanica and say, This is what you're going to do. It doesn't pass the laugh test, but the Prosecution ask you to take it seriously. Paragraph 56 of the Prosecution brief, they cite Zoran Stijovic. Again, Mr. Emmerson has done a fairly thorough demolition job on Zoran Stijovic, but I have a few more words to say. He was the MUP inspector. He was the head of the section for analysis and documentation of state security. He was, in short, a spook, a person who gathers "intelligence" by the sort of methods Mr. Guy-Smith has described. A blackmailer at best whose testimony was dripping with loathing for the KLA. We invite you to revisit his testimony in detail and to remind yourselves of how many times the Trial Chamber had to intervene to remind him to answer the question and not just keep launching into yet another prolonged diatribe against the KLA. His bias, his malice, were clear for all to see. The OTP called him apparently hoping to bolster their claim that during the indictment period the accused jointly operated a policy and practice of launching attacks on civilians or supposed collaborators. When you actually check, as both Mr. Emmerson and Mr. Guy-Smith have asked you to, and I join in that, when you check the slippery and misleading footnotes to the OTP's brief, you find, in fact, that every single one of those cases cited by Mr. Stijovic in support of his claim that innocent individuals were being targeted, every single one of them falls outside the indictment period. Not one of them has any connection with Jabllanice, and not one of them is connected in any way with any of the accused or other alleged members of the alleged JCE. At paragraphs 54 and 57 of the Prosecution brief, they cite KLA attacks on heavily armed police paramilitary forces as if they were aimed at the harmless unarmed bobby standing outside the Old Bailey. This is not the real world. Colonel Crosland and numerous other witnesses in the first trial gave clear and compelling testimony about the true nature of the heavily militarised Serbian police force, the extent to which it was integrated into Serbian war against the Kosovo Liberation Army and how out of control many of those Serbian police and their undisciplined paramilitary auxiliaries were. There is not the unarmed bobby on the beat. At paragraph 76 the OTP say in their brief that by July 1998, DB intelligence, that reliable and impartial source, "strongly indicated" that members of the KLA in the Dukagjin Zone had kidnapped and killed Serbs, Roma, and Albanians who refused to join the KLA. Is this the new standard of proof strongly indicated, Serbian intelligence, unsourced hearsay, evidence obtained by torture? From the most biased commentator imaginable. It is a strong indication, we say, of how weak the OTP case is. Where might you expect to find the hard evidence that KLA forces in the Dukagjin Zone generally, and in Jabllanice particularly, had the intention to set up a detention centre, however makeshift, or a plan to murder, torture, and mistreat Serb civilians, Catholics, Roma, Montenegrins, power supply workers, and all the rest? You would surely expect that if any such plan of any type were to exist, you would find it in the records held of meetings on June the 21st, 23rd, 24th, and you have those meetings and they're quite thoroughly and fully documented. People's organisational responsibilities are set out, but it's not there. These are exhibits P190, 191, 192, 195. There is nothing like it to be found in those exhibits. Still less is there anything in those minutes to suggest that Lahi Brahimaj was in charge of dealing with collaborators or that Jabllanice was the place where this was to be done. It's not there anywhere and I'll come back -- I'll move on to the opposite, which actually comes out of these documents. Lahi Brahimaj is appointed deputy head of the Dukagjin Zone on June 23rd, but within days it becomes clear that this is a mistake. This is a job that he is not in a position to undertake because he's not even there. I refer you to Exhibit P218. He is not there, and he is dismissed by Mr. Haradinaj after a meeting on July 1st where it's said that Mr. Brahimaj is going to have to be reprimanded for failing to fulfil his duties and attend meetings after a warning issued on July 4th, and then a prompt termination on July 5th where Mr. Lahi Brahimaj is replaced by Mr. Nazmi Brahimaj as deputy commander of the Dukagjin Zone. The question is: Where is Lahi? Once again you have the drip, drip, drip of constant repetition. It must have been Lahi Brahimaj who was responsible for everything that happened or is alleged to have happened in Jabllanice. Why? Why must it be Lahi Brahimaj? Who sign the documents warning Witness 6 that any further misconduct on his part would result in punishment? Not Lahi Brahimaj. That was Nazmi on the 25th of July. Who was it whom Rrustem Tetaj and Ramush Haradinaj met when they went to Jabllanice to see what had happened with Skender Kuqi? Even Mr. Emmerson on Monday mistakenly said at what was then page 65, line 4 -- even he mistakenly said that it was Lahi, but in fact we all know it was Nazmi Brahimaj. Rrustem Tetaj said clearly when asked by me - that's Exhibit P75, transcript page 3820: "Q. On the two occasions, when you went to Jabllanice to inquire about Skender Kuqi, there was no sign of Lahi Brahimaj in Jabllanice at that time, was there? "A. No, no, no. I had no contact with him and he was not present, no." Is it perhaps the case that people at the time in the -- I'm being told to slow down a bit. Am I rattling on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You probably are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Okay. I did take the precaution of providing our LiveNote reporters with copies of what I planned to say and I've said I've more or less struck to transcript but I'll slow down a bit conscious of the time. Is it perhaps the case that people at the time in a confused war situation simply didn't know who was in charge in Jabllanice, simply didn't know at that time who was whom? Can you afford to ignore the obvious point that with the arrest seven years ago of Lahi Brahimaj with the media attention which this understandably generated in Kosovo and with the protracted history of the first trial people today have managed to convince themselves that they saw him, whereas in fact it could have been any one of other uniformed KLA soldiers in Jabllanice at the time? But of course, say the Prosecution, Lahi was the leader of Jabllanice. Of course, say the Prosecution, Lahi was the uncle of Ramush and, therefore, it must have been Lahi. Well, this doesn't mean that Lahi Brahimaj had nothing to do with Jabllanice. Of course we're not suggesting any of the sort. But we are asking you to bear in mind the reality of the time when the KLA, during this indictment period, are gradually trying to build up a General Staff inside the country. The problem the Prosecution does not attempt to address is the practical reality of Lahi's true role and responsibilities. Bislim Zyrapi and Jakup Krasniqi testified that his responsibilities required him to be in the Berisha mountains most of the time. Yet the Prosecution say he was nearly constantly in Jabllanice, nearly constantly present. Why you have to ask. You don't even need to look at Bislim Zyrapi and Jakup Krasniqi. Why is Ramush, his own nephew, saying, You're not up to it, Lahi. You're out of here. Because he's not attending meetings. He's not physically present. There has been gross misrepresentation of the actual testimony that you have heard and that is therefore much easier to point out than the misrepresentations by the witnesses themselves in some respects. The Prosecution kicks off at paragraph 4 of their brief citing Colonel Crosland for the proposition that from April to September the Dukagjin Zone was mainly under the control of the KLA. In fact, his testimony, very forceful and powerful and compelling testimony it was, was that it was a "fluid situation." And he said that time and time again. In that situation, the Serbs could take control, he said, whenever they chose. The situation was "extremely fluid throughout, because no one side really held ground apart from the garrison towns and things like that." That's at Exhibit P8, transcript 3030, lines 1 to 2, on 20th of April, 2007. Colonel Crosland accepted that from March to July 1998: "the apparent efficacy of the KLA and control has been or was exaggerated in the minds of others where in fact on the ground it was fairly thin." Again, Prosecution Exhibit 8, T3032, lines 5 to 11, and 3033, lines 1 to 2. On Monday, Mr. Rogers again misrepresented the truth in this case and attempted, we say, to mislead you by citing a briefing given by Colonel Crosland in April 1998, and I refer to transcript page 2751, lines 8 to 11, where that misrepresentation occurred in echoing as it does paragraph 46 of the Prosecution's brief. Mr. Rogers cited the briefing given by Colonel Crosland in support of his general proposition - Mr. Rogers' general proposition - that the KLA murdered six Albanians deemed Serb sympathisers. However, what Colonel Crosland in fact said was six bodies were found in a forest near Orahovac on the 6th of April. One plausible explanation is that these were Albanians loyal to the Serbian regime killed by the KLA, but no one has claimed responsibility. Is that where we're at, one plausible explanation is cited as convincing proof beyond a reasonable doubt of something that happened near Orahovac, not in -- not near Jabllanice? Mr. Guy-Smith also drew attention to what Colonel Crosland in fact said. I would add only this, when he said - I'm quoting again from Colonel Crosland in the Limaj case: "We did see the bodies, but there was really no conclusive evidence as to how they came there and who had shot whom. This is all part of - I said the fluid situation - that prevailed throughout 1998 and 1999." That's Prosecution Exhibit 9 under seal, T1882. I make that point because not only is this in the Limaj case where counsel in this case did not have a chance to cross-examine had they wished to do so, but this wasn't even cross-examination. This was in response to the OTP Prosecutor at that time. This is evidence in chief, not led -- not in respond to a leading Defence question. Other counsel have also commented on paragraph 101 with this completely misleading statement that days before the 19th of May Serb attack, dot, dot, dot. This is in relation to Count 1 when the three left Dollc, days before the 19 of May Serb attack, paragraph 101. And in a footnote the OTP cites to Witness 66 who as you have heard does not say anything about days before the 19th, he says on the 19th, at 9.30 in the morning. His testimony quite explicitly not only says it's the 19th, he said it was a Tuesday, and I ask you to take judicial notice and we can all zip back through our computerised calendars and find out that indeed on the 19th of May, 1998, it was a Tuesday. This attempt by the OTP to reconcile these witnesses with Witness 80's testimony is at best inaccurate and at worst a deliberate misrepresentation of the evidence before you. As Mr. Emmerson has said, it means that you cannot rely on any of these footnotes, unfortunately, to support the positions they stand for or they purport to stand or. The only reason they claim it was days before is so they can tie it to one of the many different pick 'n' mix versions told by Witness 80, the story they want you to swallow. This brings me to review the gross misrepresentations that have been made to you by a number of witnesses, because we don't like the word "lie," do we. The failure to exercise any responsibility in relation to the quality of the evidence presented before you is, frankly, insulting to the intelligence of this Trial Chamber and to the integrity of this institution as a whole. The total failure to explain in their final brief what weight should be attached to the testimony of witnesses who have clear motives to lie and exaggerate, it beggars belief. Their bland shoulder-shrugging abandonment of Witness 81. Well, never mind, just ignore him. This is not the conduct of a responsible Prosecution. A responsible Prosecution would never have put Witness 81 before you in the first place. The repeated presentation of flawed testimony is the one consistent theme in the Prosecution case in this partial retrial. Your Honours may be of a generation to remember Simon and Garfunkel's "The Boxer," a man hears what he wants to hear and disregards the rest. You may also remember the chorus of that song: "lie, lie, lie, lie, lie." It's the constant drip of Prosecution's misrepresentations. Witness 6 not that we put him forward as a witness of truth in general terms, but even he claims and probably did spend the longest time of any in Jabllanice. He never mentions word one about people being put in a basement full of water. He never saw anybody beat Witness 3. He says, in terms, Witness 3 was not beaten. Mr. Guy-Smith has set out many of the details of the conflicts between Witness 6 and Witness 80, and we adopt Mr. Guy-Smith's answers -- points in their entirety. Witness 6 flatly contradicts much of the key evidence on which the Prosecution relies from Witness 3, Witness 75, and Witness 80. That doesn't matter. As long as you pick out the flavours in the pick 'n' mix bag that the OTP asks you to like. For example, paragraph 87 of the Prosecution brief. It's a little throwaway line there that Mr. Jah Bushati was forced to join the KLA. Not according to Witness 75 he wasn't. There's no evidence from Witness 80 or anyone else on that point. It's just a bold unsupported assertion. Paragraph 91. Jabllanice was a no-go area for Serbs. Colonel Crosland said there was no such thing as a no-go area. Whenever they wanted to, the Serbs were capable of overrunning Jabllanice, and they did so at least twice during the indictment period on the 2nd of August when they butchered Lahi Brahimaj's mother and grandmother, literally cutting them to pieces. Count 1, as Mr. Guy-Smith has rightly said, the question is not when these three young men were taken to Jabllanice but whether they ever were.

You've heard from Jakup Krasniqi. You have heard the evidence that of course the headquarters that they were trying to set up for the General Staff of the KLA were in the Berisha mountains. You have heard that Lahi was responsible for finance and logistics. You heard, therefore, that he had duties that compelled him to be wherever the General Staff might be at any given time. Therefore, it is perhaps not at all surprising that within a very, very few days of his supposed appointment of his actual appointment as deputy commander it is recognised that this is, frankly, a mistake, that it's not possible for him to carry that out, and we can see - if we could have Exhibit P218, please - the result of that. Thank you. And this, as Your Honours see, is the next day from the previous exhibit. That was the 4th of July. This is the 5th of July. Lahi Brahimaj is discharged from the service of the deputy commander of the Dukagjin operative headquarters, and Nazmi Brahimaj is appointed as deputy commander in his place. This order comes into effect immediately. So, Your Honours, I think it's important to focus on this point, because the constant or near constant presence claimed by the OTP of Lahi Brahimaj in Jabllanice, that his command responsibility there - this gives the lie, the exhibits put in by the Prosecution give the lie to that claim. Doesn't mean -- as I say, I'm being realistic, I hope. It doesn't mean that Lahi Brahimaj was never in the village that he was born and grew up in. Of course he was there. But it does mean you have heard all of the evidence about the difficulties of travel by night, not being able to use the roads that were blockaded by the Serbian military forces. You have heard that it was a problem of communication throughout this period and that the headquarters were a considerable distance away in the Berisha mountains, and obviously Lahi Brahimaj was required to be there on a frequent if not regular basis. That's all I say in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before the break, I had begun to address a couple of issues in reply to a question of the Presiding Judge on Lahi Brahimaj's presence or -- presence in or absence from Jabllanice, and if Your Honours have to hand our final brief, page 11, beginning at paragraph 21, we do set this out in some detail, pointing out that in 1998, Lahi was then 28 years old and already a member of the General Staff working inside the country. We cite at paragraph 22 the evidence of Bislim Zyrapi and Jakup Krasniqi concerning the conditions under which the General Staff operated. Krasniqi, in particular, at paragraph 23 saying he had even no knowledge at all of Lahi Brahimaj until he actually entered the -- Kosovo in around June 1998 when he was appointed spokesperson, and that further down on that paragraph, members of the General Staff operated in secret, meeting irregularly at a variety of separate villages in the Berisha mountains in Drenica. And again at 24, Mr. Krasniqi and Mr. Zyrapi both confirmed that Lahi was a staff officer and, as such, not in a position to be in command of soldiers in the area. And I think that, therefore -- I hope that addresses your concerns. As I said, we do not take the absurd position that Lahi Brahimaj was never in Jabllanice. We simply say that logic makes it obvious that he has -- in order to have discharged his responsibility, he has to have been absent frequently, and indeed that is underscored by his rapid dismissal by Mr. Haradinaj from his position as deputy head of the Dukagjin Zone because he was not attending meetings when he was outside the area. Thank you. If I may also make the point that in relation, on page 12, we take the point that Jabllanice was not in and could not have been in control of all of the surrounding villages. Again drawing on what Mr. Rexhahmetaj and Mr. Zyrapi said about attempting to gain control, the other very obvious point to any of us who has any knowledge, experience, background in liberation struggles and liberation movements and how they operate is that you don't win power by bullying people when you are in a relatively weak position. You have to win their hearts and minds. And the record shows that the KLA not only won the hearts and minds, it won the war. It won the respect and love of the people, as Mr. Emmerson has pointed out. I just want to hit a couple of points in relation to Witness 80's more extravagant and incredible claims. Pages 15, 16, and 17 of our final brief. The suggestion that he was targeted because he was a member of the LDK, when on his own evidence he was not an office holder. He played no leading role. There's nothing to suggest that those who did play a leading role in that village were themselves targeted, which is what you might expect if there were any basis to that claim. It makes no sense, but that almost pales into significance by his claim that in 1998 he could set up a stronger army than the KLA. If frankly beggars belief that that could come out of his mouth which is why I asked him was he actually serious about that bizarre claim. He insisted that he was. Transcript page 2594, lines 9 through 13. And then sometimes we as lawyers, when we put a witness on the stand, have to be very good at keeping a straight face and not letting our reactions show, and Mr. Rogers did a very good job of that when Witness 80 suddenly blurted out that he had been reported to have been seen in or on top of a Serbian tank during the Serb attack on Ceskovo village. And questioned by the Prosecutor as to why he claims the KLA detained him, he said allegedly someone had gone and told him -- told them that I had participated in the attack against the Ceskovo village and I had been in the tanks of the Serbian forces. That's at transcript 2416, lines 5 to 15. By the time he came to be cross-examined on this point three days later, he strengthens his account by improving on the "him" who was told or the "them" who were told, the accused himself, Lahi Brahimaj, went all over the territory and declared that I saw, the witness, with my own eyes on top of Serb tanks. Again, a factiously bizarre invention and one that is fascinatingly close to Witness 3 who testified that he was questioned himself about he, Witness 3, being seen on top of a tank in Gjurgjevik i Madh, and that's at T1566, lines 3 through 5, and following. Since both of these witnesses have had an opportunity to discuss their evidence and since this evidence is in any event broadcast for the public to listen to or to read, we say there is every reason to treat this particular invention by Witness 80 as what Mr. Guy-Smith has called the theft of another man's life or another man's claim to what actually happened to be his experience. If I may turn, then, to the death threats which we say he claims to have been made against him, and that's at paragraph 51 of our final brief on page 21. These claims were investigating thoroughly and in detail and the documents were shown to the witness in court so that he could react to them, they were investigated by UNMIK who found that there was nothing to link this claim to the KLA. And as we have put it there, the secret life of Witness 80 is rather like "The Secret Life of Walter Mitty." He claims to have been everywhere, to have seen everything, but we submit these claims are based on invention, on lies, on what he's been told by others. And we have to bear in mind the potential for what may have been suggested to him as things that might help him to gain the benefits that he has received as a result of his testimony in this case. We have set out the lies, exaggerations and inconsistencies in detail. I'm not going to rehearse that before Your Honours. You have that in front you. I'm going to talk about his motivations for a moment. His motivation to lie was underpinned by greed and need. He had lost his job, whether he was fired, as was suggested to him, for threatening his boss with a weapon or whether he simply resigned, as he claimed. Either way, he was not able to continue as a sanitation worker. He was unable to get any other job in Kosovo. He was a widower with children to support and a history of years of arms smuggling which had finally caught up with him, resulting in him facing criminal charges. So he couldn't resort to gun-running to supplement his lack of income to make up for it. But he does have one skill, and Your Honours have seen it demonstrated very clearly. He is a man of considerable cunning, a man who is manipulative, and he put those skills to work in a sensation way. Ultimately, after he had used every conceivable dishonest employ to avoid coming here to testify in The Hague, this Trial Chamber had an opportunity to watch that cunning in operation over a period of several days. The first thing out of his mouth was a lie. He claimed that he had a doctor's certificate stating that he should be hospitalised. When you, Your Honours, asked to see that supposed doctor's certificate, it turned out that the doctor had ordered no such treatment. And over the ensuing days, his supposed illness staged a miraculous recovery. He grew in confidence and in combativeness and he was skilful in evading questions that Your Honours may have thought he found too uncomfortable to respond to. I have a section in our final brief which goes into a lot of detail about Witness 81, and it is really tempting to say, Okay, Witness 81's out of here. We don't need to consider him. I adopt everything Mr. Emmerson has so ably said about why it is important to look at the way in which the Prosecution sought to introduce evidence through that despicable witness and the nature of a Prosecution that seeks to rely on a witness of that calibre. But I do say, you'll be relieved to hear, that I think Mr. Emmerson has said it all. I adopt every word of what he said, and the only reason I'm not going to belabour the point is it's in our brief. I do ask you to read it. I do ask you not to accept the Prosecution's invitation to say, All right, we don't need to think about this at all. The real question is: What kind of a Prosecution would put a witness like that on in the first place? I want to turn, if I may, to the section of our brief on page 53 concerning the evidence which came into this trial for the first time. It had no bearing on the first trial, was never mentioned, and that concerns the disappeared person, (redacted). And Your Honours will notice that I found a nice -- I think a rather nice little quote from Graham Greene at the beginning of that section which I think describes Witness 75 particularly well: "He entered the territory of lies without a passport for return." The entire history of how this witness's testimony was obtained and elicited together with the way in which the Defence and the Trial Chamber were belatedly informed of the benefits already received and those yet expected by that witness should leave the Trial Chamber doubting every word that came from his mouth. At the very least, if it is uncorroborated by a truly reliable source, we say the only safe approach is to reject it utterly. Mr. Rogers' suggestion that this is someone who came forward out of motives of honour would be farcical if it did not lie so inappropriately and irresponsibly in the mouth of a senior Prosecutor. Your Honours, I turn to paragraphs 177 to 8 on page -- pages 54 to 55 of our brief, because I think it's important to recall how evasive and reluctant he was to discuss what he had testified to under oath in other proceedings to immigration authorities. Confronted with the proof that he had written begging for help to the OTP investigator, he tried - painfully to watch - he tried to lie his way out of it. He took shelter behind a claim that he couldn't read English, although in fact you, yourself, Mr. President, had to admonish him on one occasion at the request of the court's interpreters not to answer questions in English. You may think that his claim that he didn't understand what he, himself, had written in an e-mail, despite his denials, was an utter conspicuous lie. Like the lies that he told in order to get asylum, and when he failed in that attempt, when that asylum was denied to him, he grasped desperately at the heaven-sent opportunity to try and get support for his claim from the OTP. And despite their reluctance to admit it, that is exactly what he got. He got the most conspicuous support as an immigration attorney you could possibly hope to have in your hands to lay before a Tribunal and say please re-open the case because we now have information that this person would face threats to his life, his family, his security, if sent back. A Godsend for his immigration attorney but based, we say, on lies. Because Your Honours have had the opportunity to review what he did say to the immigration authorities in support of his asylum claim. He never said a single word about his brother being mistreated by the KLA or anybody being mistreated by the KLA. He never mentioned Jabllanice. He never mentioned the Brahimajs. It's important to ask, Why not? If it had been true, it would have been a perfectly good basis for claiming asylum. Here are these people who are accused before you of war crimes who had already finished at the time that he was testifying in 2008, at the time that that witness stood before an immigration judge and gave his testimony the first trial was over as far as the evidence was concerned and as far as the final briefs were concerned. Judgement had yet to be given. But what better opportunity, if there were any basis of truth in it, than to say to the immigration judge, In support of my asylum claim, you should know those three murdering thugs who have been on trial in The Hague, those are the ones who I'm terrified of. Lahi Brahimaj is the one who did terrible things to my brother. What better claim could you possibly have to put before an immigration judge? Not one word of it. Instead, he maintained that he was in fear because the Serbs killed his brother. Your Honours may recall the document that he filed in support of his claim which purported, fraudulently, to have been sent from Kosovo in support of the claim that the Serbs had killed his brother, and it's noteworthy that he never made any suggestion that the KLA had done it, or indeed, of course we know nothing about the ultimate fate of his brother and he said that was his reason for coming forward. He hoped to find out about the ultimate fate of his brother. That may be the only true thing he said to you, but sadly, one way or another, we are no further forward in establishing that. Instead of telling what might have been thought to be a plausible claim if there were any truth to it, he concocts this bizarre story about two rogue assassins paid by a Serbian ex-policeman who lives in Montenegro who were trying to kill him because, as he says in what looks rather suspiciously like very coached testimony, I love a democratic Kosovo, because of his claimed support for the PDK, a party in which he never actively or concretely participated. And for all of this, Defence 192 exhibit under seal at transcript page 1738 through 1743, sets out the document on which he was cross-examined and the painful answers he gave in response to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Okay. At pages 65 through 72 of our final brief, and I want to take you, if I may, particularly to page 65 to start with. Your Honours recall that Mr. Guy-Smith has referred to a number of irreconcilable contradictions in Witness 80's claims upon which the OTP bases both Counts 1 and Count 6. We have set out here a series of alternative scenarios based on the evidence given by Witness 80, and Your Honours will see we have set out five particular scenarios. Probably another five could easily be added to those but we didn't want to stretch the brief out until the crack of doom.
